newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss retailer demands labels for gene soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Swiss retailer demands labels for gene soybeans.

text.p: Switzerland's second-biggest food retailer on Monday urged European food producers to demand U.S. soybean suppliers clearly separate new genetically-altered beans from the conventional crop now being harvested.

Coop Schweiz, which has 19 percent of the Swiss retail food market, said its own surveys showed over 90 percent of consumers wanted labelling of genetically-engineered produce -- and 80 percent don't want to buy altered foodstuffs.
"We are not rejecting genetic technology but rather casting a vote for transparancy, freedom of choice and consumer value," Coop said in a statement.
"This is an appeal to food retailers and producers to tell the American soybean producers what we want, which is clear labeling," a Coop spokesman told Reuters.

Europe is due for its first shipments of genetically altered soybeans later this year, when the new U.S. harvest will include "Roundup Ready" beans developed by U.S. chemicals group Monsanto Co. to withstand its Roundup Ready herbicide.

Coop's demands came three weeks after EuroCommerce, representing food retailers and wholesalers in 20 European countries, warned that European consumers could shun the 1996 U.S. soybean harvest unless gene-modified strains are labeled.
Soy is used in some 30,000 food products such as confectionery and margarine.
U.S. and European (EU) health and safety checks have approved the use of Roundup Ready beans, but approval by non-EU member Switzerland is still pending.
The U.S. grain industry says it would be costly and impractical to try to separately handle crops that are indistinguishable from traditional varieties.
But Coop said consumers must be given a clear choice and full information about something as new as genetically-altered foodstuffs.

"Coop believes that the mixed marketing of the (Roundup Ready) soybeans and the absence of transparancy and freedom of choice is the worst possible starting point for utilising genetic technology in foodstuffs," it said.
Coop said it would continue to offer prepared food products from existing stocks of conventional soy as long as available.
Afterwards, it hoped pending Swiss approval for Roundup Ready imports would require labeling of products made with the beans.
In addition, Coop said its special line of "Natura" organic products already precluded any soy products that were genetically altered. -- Zurich Newsroom, +41-1-631 7340
